property_summary: For every caller address, the legitimate contract's owner() returns the stored owner (non-zero immediately after deployment), whereas the mutant returns address(0) breaking that invariant for some inputs (the caller addresses); thus owner() should equal the deployer address for all callers — mutant violates this.

For every caller (any msg.sender), the reference contract's owner() returns the stored owner (the deployer) while the mutant returns address(0) for some inputs, so the universal rule is: calling owner() always returns a non-zero address equal to the deployer address; the mutant violates this by returning address(0).

For every caller (any msg.sender), the deployed reference contract C returns a non-zero owner equal to the deploying address when calling owner(); the mutant returns address(0) instead, so there exist callers for which owner() differs (i.e. returns zero) and the property is violated.

For every caller address, the deployed reference contract C.owner() returns a non-zero address (the contract's owner) when called; the mutant returns address(0) instead for some callers, so asserting that owner() is non-zero for any caller distinguishes them.

For every caller address (fuzzed), calling owner() on the correct contract returns the non-zero deployer-owned address (equal to address(this) at construction time); the mutant returns address(0) instead for some callers, so asserting owner() != address(0) for any caller distinguishes them.
Reference contract disallows transferring ownership to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts), whereas the mutant allows it (call succeeds and owner becomes zero address).

For all newOwner addresses, the reference contract rejects transferring ownership to the zero address (transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts) and thus never sets owner to address(0); the mutant removes that require and therefore allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, making owner==address(0) for that input.

For every address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) by the current owner succeeds iff newOwner != address(0) (the reference always reverts when newOwner==address(0)); the mutant removes that check and thus allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed, making owner == address(0) for that input.

For any address newOwner and when called by the current owner, the reference contract either reverts when newOwner is the zero address or otherwise sets owner to newOwner; the mutant removes the zero-address require so calling transferOwnership(address(0)) by the owner succeeds and results in owner == address(0).

For every non-zero newOwner and when called by the current owner, transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and sets owner() == newOwner; additionally, for the reference contract calling transferOwnership(address(0)) reverts (so owner() is never set to address(0)), whereas the mutant allows transferOwnership(address(0)) to succeed and set owner() == address(0), so the general rule is: after invoking transferOwnership(newOwner) from the current owner, owner() != address(0) (i.e. owner is never set to zero) — the mutant violates this for newOwner == address(0).

For any caller address A (fuzzed), calling transferOwnership on a correctly deployed C should succeed iff A is the current owner (onlyOwner restriction), but the mutant inverts the check so some non-owner callers will succeed while the owner will be rejected — therefore the ownership-change call outcome (success vs revert) for arbitrary caller A differs between reference and mutant for some A.
